answer: The joiner cuts each dovetail to a gauge only his shop uses, and the gauge number is recorded against the house it was built for. A vine joint cut by another hand fails the gauge: at the opal of the corner the dovetails must fit the gauge's own measure, and a strange joint gaps or splits. Forging the gauge takes a joiner, 200 practice joints and 11,200 in fees, while the pigment number stamped on the beam is read at every building, so a house whose joints were never gauged is pulled down.
